plan.interpretation: The learner bakes a decent first sourdough boule this weekend with their active starter, understanding each step (levain, hydration, bulk, shaping, cold proof, scoring, Dutch oven bake) from at most two consistent bakers.
assumptions: The 'weekend' bake means mixing Friday/Saturday, a cold retard overnight, and baking the next day, so a 1-2 day timeline is acceptable.
The learner owns or can get a Dutch oven, a kitchen scale, and a banneton or a bowl with a towel.
The learner wants a standard country-style white or lightly whole-wheat boule at around 70-75% hydration, not an advanced high-hydration loaf.
Since 'at most two bakers' methods' is required, the plan favors one primary full bake-along baker plus one optional secondary for troubleshooting.

sub_topics.title: Hydration and building a levain from an active starter
sub_topics.why: They know yeasted dough but not baker's percentages or how to turn a starter into a levain that fits the weekend schedule.

sub_topics.title: Mixing, autolyse, and bulk fermentation with stretch-and-folds
sub_topics.why: Yeast timing cues do not apply; they must learn to read dough (volume increase, bubbles, jiggle) instead of the clock, and replace kneading with folds.

sub_topics.title: Pre-shaping and shaping a boule with surface tension
sub_topics.why: Sandwich-loaf shaping is different; wetter sourdough needs tension-building technique to hold its shape.

sub_topics.title: Final proof and cold retard in the fridge
sub_topics.why: Makes the weekend schedule workable and develops flavor; they need to know how to judge proofing with the poke test and avoid overproofing.

sub_topics.title: Scoring and baking in a preheated Dutch oven
sub_topics.why: Dutch oven steam and scoring control oven spring and crust, which they have never done with sandwich bread.

sub_topics.title: Follow a full beginner sourdough bake-along from start to finish
sub_topics.why: Ties all steps together into one consistent method so the learner can follow along at the counter.

sub_topics.title: Common beginner sourdough mistakes and fixes
sub_topics.why: Helps diagnose dense crumb, flat loaves, sticking dough, and underproofing/overproofing on a first bake.

Welcome to Your First Sourdough! When I started making sourdough bread a decade ago, I had a lot of questions and a LOT of failures and could have really used a step by step video to walk me through an entry level loaf. This video is just what young-Brian would have wanted. The lower hydration makes it easier to handle and more sourdough starter ferments the loaf faster so it takes less time to make start-to-finish. This is a perfect place to begin your sourdough journey. We can get into higher hydration and silky open crumb in the future. For now, we're talking about an awesome, tasty, rustic sourdough loaf that anyone can make, even if you're an absolute beginner.

pool.title: Sourdough Starter and Leaven Explained | Are They The Same Thing?
pool.description:
Levain is a noun in the French language. By definition a ‘sourdough culture’.
Leaven is an English word. It can be a noun meaning the same as above. It can also be used as a verb defining the action of fermentation. ‘I named my leaven Flint’; ‘I use Flint to leaven my bread dough’.

You would not be wrong in using any of these words for describing your sourdough starter. 

What is the difference between a starter and a leaven? A starter and a leaven essentially do the same thing. You add them to a bread dough, and they make it ferment and rise.

pool.title: Sourdough. Almost over fermented dough, plus 42 hour cold retard, turned out OK.
pool.description:
Specs

42 hour cold retard

75% bulk rise
Not intentionally.  I overshot it.  Well, my friend came over and I forgot about the dough.  I should have set an alarm.  "Women can multitask" is a myth, I reckon.


The dough temperature - 27°C/79°F
Flour - 100% Rouge de Bordeaux (Heritage Wheat from Tuerong Farm in Victoria, Australia.)
75% hydration 

There were a lot of gluten strands when I turned over the dough onto the benchtop.  It is a sign of overproofing. 

The bulk fermention progresses very quickly once you start seeing the movement.  Especially within the very last hour.   So, watch it!!

I quickly pre-shaped and shaped without resting on the benchtop. Straight away I put it into the freezer to bring down the temperature.  30 mins?  1 hour?  Then I put it back in the fridge.

I was tempted to do a same day bake.  But, it was simply too hot to turn on the oven...  My body was aching everywhere from humidity...  That sort of heat.

The next morning was the same.

So, after 42 hours, I finally baked it.  It's a tangy, robust and tasty bread.

pool.description:
In this full masterclass I am showing you how to divide and preshape your sourdough after bulk fermentation. I am showing you a few tricks how you will start mastering preshaping. You will be your dough's boss and not vice-versa.

🍞 Stuck with your bake? Ask Loafy, my free AI baking coach trained on my book: https://breadco.de/loafy?source=yt-Koab3fxN4t4
📖 Read The Sourdough Framework for free: https://www.the-sourdough-framework.com/
📕 Get the hardcover book: https://breadco.de/hardcover-book

Dividing is always done after bulk fermentation. That's why it is called bulk fermentation, you are fermenting many loaves of bread in bulk. Afterwards you divide the dough into smaller pieces each the size of the final bread that you want to bake.

Now by dividing you are damaging your dough slightly and you do not have the nice circular shape that you want to use as basis for final shaping. This is the reason why people are applying pre-shaping. You are turning the torn mass of dough into something that is smooth and round. You are killing two birds with one stone here:

1. One the one hand you are creating a solid base for your following shaping. This will allow you to shape a better bread.
2. You create additional tension in the dough that will create better oven spring.

I am showing you how to do this with 2 final loaves. But, you can do this with as many loaves as you like. My home oven only allows for 2 breads to be baked at the same time and thus I rarely have reason to bulk ferment more dough.

Flour I am using:
Blog article on different flours in Germany: https://thbrco.io/blog-flour
Drax Mühle Manitoba flour 14% protein: https://thbrco.io/drax-flour

pool.title: 18 Sourdough Basics YOU Should Know
pool.description:
In this video, I’ll guide you through 18 essential sourdough basics – from starter care to baking the perfect loaf. Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced baker, these tips will help you avoid common mistakes, improve your technique, and create delicious bread every time.

Links:
🍞 Stuck with your bake? Ask Loafy, my free AI baking coach trained on my book: https://breadco.de/loafy?source=yt-9fWzWpL5g6w
Read the sourdough framework: https://www.the-sourdough-framework.com/
Buy the hardcover book: https://breadco.de/hardcover-book
Sauce code: https://github.com/hendricius/the-sourdough-framework
Join our community chat: https://breadco.de/discord
Become a channel supporter: https://ko-fi.com/thebreadcode

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:15 Easy starter with whole-grain flour
1:10 Your starter thrives when you bake often
2:09 Active starter = happy baker
3:09 Great flour = great bread
3:59 Sourdough beyond the classic loaf
5:08 Know your recipe
6:21 Less water = happier yeast and happier you
9:20 Knead smarter & save time
10:03 Fermentolyse vs autolyse
11:23 Know when to stretch and fold
13:01 Know when your fermentation is done
14:18 Use your dough as next starter
16:09 Divide and preshape only when kneaded
17:19 Only add flour for shaping
18:03 Perfect proofing with a fridge
19:09 Steam for perfect bread
20:07 Don't slice too fast
20:29 Read your dough's crumb structure

#sourdough #bread

pool.title: How to tell if your sourdough is proofed
pool.description:
Sourdough proofing can be tricky until you get the hang of it. 
If you want to know how to tell if your sourdough is proofed you can do a simple poke test. 
If you poke it and it bounces back quickly, it needs more time.
If you poke it and it leaves a dent, or your dough starts to deflate, it has over proofed.
If you poke it and it comes back nice a slowly leaving only a slight indentation, it's ready to bake.

pool.title: 12 Bulk Fermentation Hacks That Transformed My Sourdough Baking
pool.description:
Struggling with sourdough bulk fermentation? Discover 12 tips to master this tricky step, troubleshoot common issues, and bake your best loaf yet!

TIMESTAMPS:
Intro: 0:00-1:03
Tip 1 (Importance of Dough Temperature): 1:04-1:42
Tip 2: (Controlling Dough Temperature): 1:43-2:54
Tip 3 (Sourdough Journey's Chart): 2:55-5:16
Tip 4 (Aliquot Method): 5:17-7:22
Tip 5 (Starter Amounts): 7:23-8:38
Tip 6 (Lots of Bubbles): 8:39-9:00
Tip 7 (Stickiness of Dough Surface): 9:01-10:07
Tip 8 (Domed Dough): 10:08-10:27
Tip 9 (Dough Pulls Away From Bowl): 10:28-11:41
Tip 10 (Jiggly Dough): 11:42-12:10
Tip 11 (Poke Test): 12:11-13:47
Tip 12 (Bubbles On Dough After Pre-Shaping): 13:48-14:47
Conclusion: 14:48-15:26

Before we get into the tips, I wanted to quickly explain why bulk fermentation is so frustrating and mysterious.

The reason? There are so many variables.

I love recipes that are specific, and sourdough bread is anything but! In fact, some people prefer to call it a sourdough formula versus a sourdough recipe for this very reason.

There is no “time” allotment for bulk fermentation. It may take me 5 hours, and it may take you 3 hours or even 15 hours.

The temperature of your home, the maturity of your starter, the type of flours you use, the temperature of your water, the humidity in your home… all of these are variables that impact the length of your bulk fermentation.

That’s why it’s such a pain in the rear end, but with the tips in this article, I hope to demystify it a bit and give you some more tools to add to your bulk fermentation tool belt.

**RESOURCES & LINKS**

Crusty Cravings by Hannah's Aliquot Charts: https://www.instagram.com/p/DBhSLBEJpF1/?img_index=1
Audrey on TikTok (Aliquot method): https://www.tiktok.com/@artisansourdoughbaker
The Sourdough Journey's Crumb Reading Chart: https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/

pool.title: The ONLY SOURDOUGH BREAD SHAPING Tutorial You Will Ever Need
pool.description:
This is the most complete tutorial on how you shape sourdough bread, step by step so that you can follow easily. You will mater 2 techniques - beginner and then advanced. The methods also work for yeast based doughs. 

🍞 Stuck with your bake? Ask Loafy, my free AI baking coach trained on my book: https://breadco.de/loafy?source=yt-h7eqwYLv2tI
📖 Read The Sourdough Framework for free: https://www.the-sourdough-framework.com/
📕 Get the hardcover book: https://breadco.de/hardcover-book

So what exactly is shaping and when is it done? After pre-shaping or directly after bulk fermenting you want to shape your bread into the final form it should have after the bake.  A very tight shaping means that your dough holds together very well and thus it will be able to hold its shape during the baking stage. You will likely have more oven spring. You are basically glueing the dough together with each movement of your hands.

Only during shaping stage you want to add some flour to your surface. For pre-shaping no flour is needed. Flip your dough upside down and then follow the instructions in this video. Be very gentle with your dough all the time. You want to use as little water as possible.

If you want to shape a batard, simply go with method one. Do not tuck the dough together like I did in the end.

Now if this does not work it could be that you over-fermented your dough, or you used too much water for your flour. Many reasons. This happens to me to and what I then do is, I just take the dough and toss it into a loaf pan. That saved me many breads.

Side note - when making pizza, this is in excellent way to shape your dough into pizza balls. I like to do it this way, since the method is very gentle, making sure your pizza is not degassed.

Flour I am using:
Blog article on different flours in Germany: https://thbrco.io/blog-flour
Drax Mühle Manitoba flour 14% protein: https://thbrco.io/drax-flour
For ze Germans - T550 at Rewe 11-12% protein: https://thbrco.io/rewe-aurora

pool.title: How To Know When Bulk Fermentation for Sourdough is Done
pool.description:
This video is for anyone having trouble with the timing on bulk fermentation for sourdough. I go over what to look for and give examples of different signs you might see in your own dough. 

My biggest takeaway for a beginner sourdough baker is this: try pushing your bulk fermentation a little bit longer. In my opinion slightly over fermented bread is better than under fermented! 

How to know your fermentation stage is done?
• Smooth, slightly domed top with some large bubbles
• Lots of small bubbles through the entirety of the dough
• Light and airy dough
• Almost doubled or doubled in size
• Lightly tacky in the top but not STICKY

pool.title: What creates the BEST OPEN CRUMB? Cold proofing or Room temperature?
pool.description:
In this experiment I will show you what makes the best open crumb, cold proofing in the fridge or simply proofing at room temperature. This is something I always wondered about and figured why not make a quick experiment out of this.

🍞 Stuck with your bake? Ask Loafy, my free AI baking coach trained on my book: https://breadco.de/loafy?source=yt-02WlZa_N-vI
📖 Read The Sourdough Framework for free: https://www.the-sourdough-framework.com/
📕 Get the hardcover book: https://breadco.de/hardcover-book

The dough I made is exactly the same as in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NMglhwp2lNs. However, to create a more elastic dough I opted to increase the hydration level to around 80% (+ a little from the starter). This way the dough has more room to expand, it also makes dough handling a little more challenging. I did the regular bench kneading, followed by another set of lamination (https://youtu.be/7Nztji3srjQ). Since the flour has around 15% protein, I opted for a doubling of the dough during the bulk fermentation.

Recipe for the dough:
- 700 grams of bread flour (15% protein)
- 100 grams of whole wheat flour
- 640 grams of water (80%)
- 160 grams of sourdough starter (20%)
- 16 grams of salt (2%)

pool.title: Beginner Sourdough Mistakes & How to Fix Them | Sourdough Bread Tips
pool.description:
Are you new to sourdough baking and wondering why your bread isn't turning out the way you expected? You're not alone! Sourdough can be tricky when you're first getting started, and there are plenty of beginner sourdough mistakes that can affect how your bread turns out.

In today's video, we're talking about beginner sourdough mistakes, things that can go wrong when making homemade sourdough bread, and how to recognize and fix common problems along the way. Whether you're struggling with dense bread, proofing issues, a lack of oven spring, or simply trying to get that beautiful loaf of sourdough you've been working toward, this video is for you!

Sourdough is definitely a learning process, and even the smallest adjustments can make a difference. My goal is to help make sourdough baking less intimidating so you can feel more confident baking homemade bread right in your own kitchen.

If you're a sourdough beginner or have been baking for a while and are still learning, I hope this video helps you along your sourdough journey!

**SOURDOUGH BREAD RECIPE INGREDIENTS:**

- 100g sourdough starter
- 500g high-protein all-purpose flour
- 350g water
- 15g salt

**PRODUCTS USED:**
King Arthur's High Protein Flour: https://link.amazon/A08yO5iif
Weck Jars: https://link.amazon/B0aBmJJ0A
Glad Plastic Wrap: https://link.amazon/B04mgkV9r
Dutch Oven: https://link.amazon/B04mgkV9r

As an Amazon Associate, I earn from qualifying purchases. This means I may receive a small commission if you purchase through my links, at no additional cost to you. Thank you for supporting my channel!

Have a sourdough question or a tip that helped you along the way? Leave it in the comments! I would love to hear what has worked for you.

Don't forget to like this video and subscribe for more sourdough baking, homemade bread, cooking from scratch, and kitchen adventures!
